title: How Opening Traps Actually Work
summary: Every trap in this library is one of three ideas. Learn the three and you will spot the rest on your own.

sections.heading: The thing they have in common
sections.body: A trap is not a clever move. It is a position where the natural move loses, and your opponent is betting that you will play naturally. That is why memorising refutations is a weak defence and recognising the setup is a strong one — there are hundreds of traps and only a handful of setups.

sections.heading: Idea 1: the square only the king defends
sections.body: f7 for Black and f2 for White are defended by the king alone at the start of the game. Point two pieces at that square before the defender has developed and you have a real threat, because the king cannot recapture without walking into the open. Scholar's Mate, the Fried Liver, and the refutation of 2...f6 are all the same idea wearing different clothes. The counting rule is blunt and reliable: after every enemy move, ask how many pieces attack f7 and how many defend it.

diagram.caption: Two attackers on f7, one defender. From here every black move that does not address f7 loses immediately.

sections.heading: Idea 2: the free material that isn't
sections.body: Your opponent leaves something hanging. It is hanging because taking it costs you more than the piece is worth — usually a tempo, a file, or your king's safety. The Blackburne Shilling gives you a whole pawn to lure a knight off guard duty; Legal's Mate gives you a whole queen. The habit that beats all of them is one question asked before every capture: what is their reply? Not what is mine — what is theirs.

sections.heading: Idea 3: the pin that is not a pin
sections.body: A piece pinned to the king cannot legally move. A piece pinned to the queen absolutely can, and if moving it creates a bigger threat than the queen is worth, it will. Legal's Mate is the famous case: the knight is 'pinned' to the queen, it moves anyway, and three minor pieces deliver mate while the queen sits untouched on d1. Whenever you rely on a pin, check whether it is legal or merely uncomfortable.

sections.heading: The defensive habit that covers all three
sections.body: Before each move, in this order: what does my opponent's last move attack; what does my intended move leave undefended; and what is their best reply. That takes about five seconds and defuses nearly every trap in club chess. The Test drills in this app stop the moment you skip it, and the replay shows you the exact move where you did.
